claim: Choanoflagellates are the closest living unicellular relatives to metazoans.
source: Choanoflagellates are unicellular (or colonial) organisms within the Opisthokonta branch that share a last common ancestor with metazoans (the urchoanozoan) more than 600 million years ago (Carr et al., 2008; King, 2004; Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Steenkamp et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature (Carr et al., 2008; King, 2004; Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Steenkamp et al., 2006).

claim: Choanoflagellates and metazoans shared a last common ancestor more than 600 million years ago.
source: Choanoflagellates are unicellular (or colonial) organisms within the Opisthokonta branch that share a last common ancestor with metazoans (the urchoanozoan) more than 600 million years ago (Carr et al., 2008; King, 2004; Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Steenkamp et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature (Carr et al., 2008; King, 2004; Ruiz-Trillo et al., 2008; Steenkamp et al., 2006).

claim: S. rosetta cells contain a single flagellum surrounded by a ring of 25-36 actin-based microvilli.
source: S. rosetta cells contain a single flagellum, which extends from the cell body and is surrounded by a ring of 25–36 actin-based microvilli (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—video 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Dayel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by data shown in figures and a citation to Dayel et al., 2011.

claim: Choanoflagellates use the planar beat of their flagellum to generate both cell motility and microcurrents for engulfing bacterial prey.
source: As microbial filter feeders, choanoflagellates use the planar beat of their flagellum to generate both cell motility and microcurrents, which enable them to more easily engulf bacterial prey (Pettitt et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pettitt et al., 2002.

claim: The choanoflagellate flagellum has a 9+2 axonemal microtubule arrangement.
source: The overall structure of the choanoflagellate flagellum has been previously studied using light and conventional electron microscopy techniques, revealing a 9+2 axonemal microtubule arrangement and a basal body that is surrounded by a microtubule rootlet structure (Karpov, 2016; Karpov and Leadbeater, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karpov, 2016 and Karpov and Leadbeater, 1998.

claim: The choanoflagellate basal body is surrounded by a microtubule rootlet structure.
source: The overall structure of the choanoflagellate flagellum has been previously studied using light and conventional electron microscopy techniques, revealing a 9+2 axonemal microtubule arrangement and a basal body that is surrounded by a microtubule rootlet structure (Karpov, 2016; Karpov and Leadbeater, 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Karpov, 2016 and Karpov and Leadbeater, 1998.

claim: Cryo-FIB milling and cryo-ET were used to generate ~150-200 nm thin lamellae of plunge-frozen S. rosetta cells.
source: During plunge-freezing, areas close to the cell body were embedded in relatively thick ice (>500 nm); therefore, we used cryo-FIB milling to generate ~150–200 nm thin lamellae (sections) of the plunge-frozen cells before cryo-ET imaging (Figure 2A-C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and methods described in the manuscript and shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The S. rosetta basal apparatus contains a basal body and a surrounding MTOC ring of dense material from which lateral rootlet microtubules radiate outwards.
source: Within the reconstruction of the basal apparatus, we observe part of the basal body and the surrounding MTOC ring of dense material from which the lateral rootlet microtubules radiate outwards (Figure 2E; Karpov, 2016; Pozdnyakov et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2E and citations to Karpov, 2016 and Pozdnyakov et al., 2017.

claim: Flagellar vane filaments were clearly visible on two opposite sides of the S. rosetta flagellum and extended to the edges of the imaging area (~3 µm).
source: In addition, the flagellar vane filaments were clearly visible on two opposite sides of the flagellum and extended to the edges of the imaging area (~3 µm) (Figure 2D and F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2D and F.

claim: Subtomogram averaging of >7500 axonemal repeats from 54 cryo-tomograms yielded an average with 2.2 nm resolution.
source: To better resolve the molecular details of the S. rosetta flagellum, we performed subtomogram averaging of >7500 axonemal repeats (96 nm length) that were extracted from 54 cryo-tomograms (Figure 2G, green brackets; Figure 3), which yielded an average with 2.2 nm resolution (0.5 FSC criterion; Figure 3—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and Table 1.

claim: S. rosetta flagellar axonemal repeats contain outer dynein arms with two motor domains each.
source: With this resolution, we observe that the axonemal repeats of S. rosetta flagella contain outer dynein arms with two motor domains each, the double-headed I1 (f) inner dynein complex, and six single-headed inner dynein arms, a, b, c, e, g, and d (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: S. rosetta flagella contain the double-headed I1 (f) inner dynein complex.
source: With this resolution, we observe that the axonemal repeats of S. rosetta flagella contain outer dynein arms with two motor domains each, the double-headed I1 (f) inner dynein complex, and six single-headed inner dynein arms, a, b, c, e, g, and d (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: S. rosetta flagella contain six single-headed inner dynein arms: a, b, c, e, g, and d.
source: With this resolution, we observe that the axonemal repeats of S. rosetta flagella contain outer dynein arms with two motor domains each, the double-headed I1 (f) inner dynein complex, and six single-headed inner dynein arms, a, b, c, e, g, and d (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The ODAs and a subset of IDAs (b, c, and e) on DMT 5 of the S. rosetta flagellum are replaced by the o-SUB5-6 and i-SUB5-6 structures.
source: Similar to sea urchin sperm flagella (Lin et al., 2012b), the ODAs and a subset of IDAs (b, c, and e) on DMT 5 of the S. rosetta flagellum are replaced by the o-SUB5-6 and i-SUB5-6 structures (Figure 3—figure supplement 2; DMT5, green and orange arrowheads), thus allowing us to unambiguously determine the doublet numbers DMT1-9 within each reconstructed flagellum (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 and citation to Lin et al., 2012b.

claim: A unique connection exists between the A-tubule and the base of IDA c on DMT 9 in S. rosetta flagella.
source: We also observed a unique connection between the A-tubule and the base of IDA c on DMT 9, with a smaller partial density near the base of the A-tubule on DMT 1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2, dark yellow arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The positional flexibility of radial spoke heads in S. rosetta was likely because intact cells were frozen while their flagella were actively beating.
source: This positional flexibility was likely because intact S. rosetta cells were frozen while their flagella were actively beating.
evidence: Based on inference from experimental conditions.

claim: The shape of S. rosetta radial spoke heads resembles narrow ice skates, similar to sea urchin and mammalian cilia and flagella.
source: Similar to sea urchin and mammalian cilia and flagella, the shape of the S. rosetta radial spoke heads resemble narrow ice skates (Figure 3C'and F; Figure 4), rather than the broad radial spoke head morphology of other unicellular species like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena (Figure 4; Barber et al., 2012; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2014; Pigino et al., 2011; Pigino et al., 2012; Poghosyan et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4, and citations to multiple studies.

claim: The radial spoke head morphology of Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena is broad.
source: Similar to sea urchin and mammalian cilia and flagella, the shape of the S. rosetta radial spoke heads resemble narrow ice skates (Figure 3C'and F; Figure 4), rather than the broad radial spoke head morphology of other unicellular species like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena (Figure 4; Barber et al., 2012; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2014; Pigino et al., 2011; Pigino et al., 2012; Poghosyan et al., 2020; Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4 and citations to multiple studies.

claim: The head domains of S. rosetta RS1 and RS2 are separated from one another.
source: The head domains of S. rosetta RS1 and RS2 are separated from one another, whereas those of RS2 and RS3 are connected (Figure 3C, E, and F, Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The head domains of S. rosetta RS2 and RS3 are connected.
source: The head domains of S. rosetta RS1 and RS2 are separated from one another, whereas those of RS2 and RS3 are connected (Figure 3C, E, and F, Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Many conserved MIP structures were identified within the S. rosetta flagellar doublet microtubules, including MIPs 1a, 1b, 2a, 2b, 2c, 3a, 3b, and 6a-d.
source: Based on their locations and periodicities along the 96 nm repeat, we identified many conserved MIP structures within the S. rosetta flagellar doublet microtubules, including MIPs 1 a, 1b, 2 a, 2b, 2 c, 3 a, 3b, and 6a-d (Figure 5, A-F).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: In S. rosetta, MIP1a is shorter than MIP1b.
source: MIP1a is typically longer than MIP1b in other species (Song et al., 2020), but in S. rosetta, MIP1a is shorter than MIP1b (Figure 5, A-B, D-E).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5 and citation to Song et al., 2020.

claim: A previously unobserved ~3.5 nm wide filamentous MIP, named rail-MIP, was identified in S. rosetta flagella.
source: Furthermore, we identified a previously unobserved ~3.5 nm wide filamentous MIP, here named rail-MIP, which runs along the length of the A-tubule near protofilament A13 and seems to connect to MIP 6ab (Figure 5A and G, class 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The rail-MIP runs along the length of the A-tubule near protofilament A13 and seems to connect to MIP 6ab.
source: Furthermore, we identified a previously unobserved ~3.5 nm wide filamentous MIP, here named rail-MIP, which runs along the length of the A-tubule near protofilament A13 and seems to connect to MIP 6ab (Figure 5A and G, class 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The rail-MIP was present in only 39% of all averaged axonemal repeat units.
source: Indeed, these analyses revealed that the rail-MIP was not ubiquitously present: only 39% of all averaged axonemal repeat units contained the rail-MIP, and its presence was enriched in DMTs 5–7 (Figure 5G, class 2 and table), as compared to doublets 1–4 and 8–9, which mostly lacked the rail-MIP (Figure 5G, class 1 and table).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The presence of rail-MIP was enriched in DMTs 5-7.
source: Indeed, these analyses revealed that the rail-MIP was not ubiquitously present: only 39% of all averaged axonemal repeat units contained the rail-MIP, and its presence was enriched in DMTs 5–7 (Figure 5G, class 2 and table), as compared to doublets 1–4 and 8–9, which mostly lacked the rail-MIP (Figure 5G, class 1 and table).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The rail-MIP is present in a cryo-FIB-milled lamella containing the proximal region of the flagellum.
source: This asymmetric distribution does not appear to correlate with any other observed features (such as presence of vane, barbs, microvilli, or IFT particles), but the rail-MIP is present in a cryo-FIB-milled lamella containing the proximal region of the flagellum (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that its distribution could be related to the location of the tomogram along the length of the flagellum (proximal vs. distal).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The rail-MIP distribution could be related to the location of the tomogram along the length of the flagellum (proximal vs. distal).
source: This asymmetric distribution does not appear to correlate with any other observed features (such as presence of vane, barbs, microvilli, or IFT particles), but the rail-MIP is present in a cryo-FIB-milled lamella containing the proximal region of the flagellum (Figure 5—figure supplement 2), suggesting that its distribution could be related to the location of the tomogram along the length of the flagellum (proximal vs. distal).
evidence: Based on inference from the observed distribution pattern.

claim: S. rosetta flagellar DMTs contain one ~4 nm long hole per axonemal repeat in the inner junction between protofilaments A1 and B10.
source: Flagellar DMTs of most (wild-type) species described so far by cryo-ET display one ~4 nm long hole per axonemal repeat in the inner junction between protofilaments A1 and B10; the only described exception is the T. brucei flagellar DMTs that has an additional (more proximal) inner junction hole per repeat (Imhof et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Imhof et al., 2019 and established knowledge from cryo-ET studies.

claim: One PACRG-subunit is missing near the N-DRC base-plate from the FAP20-PACRG inner junction filament.
source: We and others have shown that one PACRG-subunit is missing near the N-DRC base-plate from the FAP20-PACRG inner junction filament (Dymek et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019; Nicastro et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dymek et al., 2019; Ma et al., 2019; Nicastro et al., 2011.

claim: S. rosetta flagella contain two additional inner junction-holes, one near the base of RS1, and one near the base of RS3.
source: In addition to this inner junction-hole near the N-DRC, S. rosetta flagella contain two additional inner junction-holes, one near the base of RS1, and one near the base of RS3 (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B and D, pink and green arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: The additional inner junction holes in S. rosetta could represent additional PACRG subunit losses.
source: Distances between the previously-reported N-DRC-related inner junction-hole and the additional proximal and distal hole are ~32 and~16 nm, respectively, suggesting that they could represent additional PACRG subunit losses, given the 8 nm periodicity of the FAP20-PACRG repeat (Dymek et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on inference from measured distances and citation to Dymek et al., 2019.

claim: S. rosetta flagellar DMTs exhibit a ~6.5 nm long gap in protofilament A2 of the A-tubule between RS3 and RS1 from the next axonemal repeat unit, likely due to a missing tubulin dimer.
source: S. rosetta flagellar DMTs also exhibit a (so far unique)~6.5 nm long gap in protofilament A2 of the A-tubule between RS3 and RS1 from the next axonemal repeat unit, likely due to a missing tubulin dimer (Figure 5H, class 2; Figure 5—figure supplement 3, B and D, olive arrowheads).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 3, with inference about the cause.

claim: The A2-hole is present in ~39% of repeats in S. rosetta flagella.
source: Our classification analyses revealed that the A2-hole is present in ~39% of repeats, including over 50% of repeats from DMTs 1, 5, and 6 and with lower frequencies in the other DMTs (Figure 5H table: class 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The S. rosetta CPC has a relatively fixed orientation.
source: Like other opisthokonts, the S. rosetta CPC has a relatively fixed orientation, and the plane that contains both CPC microtubules is roughly parallel to the 5–6 bridge (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and comparison to other opisthokonts.

claim: The plane containing both CPC microtubules in S. rosetta is roughly parallel to the 5-6 bridge.
source: Like other opisthokonts, the S. rosetta CPC has a relatively fixed orientation, and the plane that contains both CPC microtubules is roughly parallel to the 5–6 bridge (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: S. rosetta's flagellum has a planar, sinusoidal waveform with an amplitude perpendicular to the CPC and 5-6-bridge planes.
source: This orientation is consistent with S. rosetta's flagellum having a planar, sinusoidal waveform (Dayel et al., 2011; Dayel and King, 2014) with an amplitude (beating direction) that is perpendicular to the CPC and 5–6-bridge planes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Dayel et al., 2011 and Dayel and King, 2014, and inference from CPC orientation.

claim: Subtomogram averaging of >1300 CPC repeats from 28 cryo-tomograms yielded an average with 2.5 nm resolution.
source: To better resolve the molecular details of the S. rosetta CPC, we performed subtomogram averaging of >1300 repeats (32 nm length) that were extracted from 28 cryo-tomograms (selected based on best image signal-to-noise ratio) (Figure 6), which yielded an average with 2.5 nm resolution (0.5 FSC criterion) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and Table 1.

claim: The S. rosetta CPC contains all major projections described in other organisms with longitudinal periodicities of 16 nm (C1a, b; C2a, b, c, d, and e) and 32 nm (C1c, d, e, f).
source: The S. rosetta CPC contains all major projections described in other organisms with the previously described longitudinal periodicities of 16 nm (C1a, b; C2a, b, c, d, and e) and 32 nm (C1c, d, e, f) (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2; Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claim: The S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella.
source: In many ways, the S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019): both lack the C2 MIP, have a small C1e projection, and exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections, as compared to the Chlamydomonas CPC (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claim: Both S. rosetta and sea urchin CPCs lack the C2 MIP.
source: In many ways, the S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019): both lack the C2 MIP, have a small C1e projection, and exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections, as compared to the Chlamydomonas CPC (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claim: Both S. rosetta and sea urchin CPCs have a small C1e projection.
source: In many ways, the S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019): both lack the C2 MIP, have a small C1e projection, and exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections, as compared to the Chlamydomonas CPC (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claim: Both S. rosetta and sea urchin CPCs exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections.
source: In many ways, the S. rosetta CPC strongly resembles that of sea urchin sperm flagella (Carbajal-González et al., 2013; Fu et al., 2019): both lack the C2 MIP, have a small C1e projection, and exhibit prominent connections between the C1a and C2a projections, as compared to the Chlamydomonas CPC (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citations to Carbajal-González et al., 2013 and Fu et al., 2019.

claim: The S. rosetta CPC exhibits partial reduction of the C1d protein network, specifically it seems that FAP54 is lacking.
source: One unique feature of the S. rosetta CPC, however, is the partial reduction of the C1d protein network, specifically it seems that FAP54 is lacking (Han et al., 2022), which exposes a larger area of the C1 microtubule wall (Figure 6, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 2, and citation to Han et al., 2022.

claim: Vane filaments were clearly observed extending from the flagellar membrane on either side of the S. rosetta flagellum.
source: In contrast to previous studies in which vane preservation was an issue, we clearly observed vane filaments extending from the flagellar membrane on either side of the flagellum in S. rosetta, both in the cryo-FIB lamella of the proximal flagellar region (Figure 2, D and F; Figure 5—figure supplement 2A), as well as more distally, where the flagellum is embedded in ice thin enough to be directly imaged using cryo-ET (Figure 2G, Figure 7).
evidence: Supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The vane originates at the base of the flagellum.
source: The vane originates at the base of the flagellum, and its edges often extend the entire width of (and beyond) our tomograms and lamella, which are ~1.2 µm (tomograms) to ~3 µm (lamella) wide (Figure 2D–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The vane edges often extend the entire width of (and beyond) the tomograms and lamella.
source: The vane originates at the base of the flagellum, and its edges often extend the entire width of (and beyond) our tomograms and lamella, which are ~1.2 µm (tomograms) to ~3 µm (lamella) wide (Figure 2D–G, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A, Figure 7, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The plane containing the vane appears to be oriented parallel to the ice layer in which the sample is embedded, likely due to surface tension forces during blotting.
source: In our data, the plane containing the vane varies in relation to the CPC/sub-5–6 planes, and instead appears to be oriented parallel to the ice layer in which the sample is embedded, likely due to surface tension forces during blotting (Figure 6—figure supplement 1J-K).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1J-K and inference about the cause.

claim: The vane orientation is consistent with its predicted physiological function in the pumping mechanism of filter feeders.
source: This orientation is consistent with the vane's predicted physiological function in the pumping mechanism of these filter feeders (Nielsen et al., 2017), as the vane would be naturally positioned to experience hydrodynamic drag, pushing liquid and prey close to the collar (Figure 6—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nielsen et al., 2017 and inference from observed orientation.

claim: The S. rosetta flagellar vane is composed of two sheets of thin filaments on either side of the flagellum.
source: Our data suggest that the S. rosetta flagellar vane is composed of two sheets of thin filaments on either side of the flagellum, which extend from the flagellar membrane for approximately 80 nm before they split and attach to neighboring filaments to form diamond-shaped meshes (Figure 7A-D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: Vane filaments extend from the flagellar membrane for approximately 80 nm before they split and attach to neighboring filaments to form diamond-shaped meshes.
source: Our data suggest that the S. rosetta flagellar vane is composed of two sheets of thin filaments on either side of the flagellum, which extend from the flagellar membrane for approximately 80 nm before they split and attach to neighboring filaments to form diamond-shaped meshes (Figure 7A-D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A-D.

claim: One or two rows of 'nodes' are visible near the flagellar membrane where the vane filaments first branch.
source: One or two rows of 'nodes' are visible near the flagellar membrane where the filaments first branch (Figure 2F, Figure 7A, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in multiple figures.

claim: The two sheets of vane filaments and the nodes are separated by ~45 nm.
source: Because our reconstructions are three dimensional, we can view these nodes rotated 90 degrees around the x-axis, which clearly shows that the two sheets of vane filaments and the nodes are separated by ~45 nm (Figure 7A, inset).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A inset.

claim: The nodes of the vane filaments are offset from one another so that the vertices of the diamonds from one sheet are centered within the diamonds from the overlaying sheet when viewed from top down.
source: The nodes of the vane filaments are offset from one another so that the vertices of the diamonds from one sheet are centered within the diamonds from the overlaying sheet when viewed from top down (Figure 7A and C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7A and C.

claim: Some regions of S. rosetta flagella have vane filaments that are highly organized and interconnected, whereas others have wispy, individual filaments.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we observed some regions with vane filaments that were highly organized and interconnected, whereas others appeared to have wispy, individual filaments (Figure 7B-D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Vane filaments were apparent in all but one of the 54 tomograms analyzed.
source: Vane filaments were apparent in all but one of the 54 tomograms we analyzed, with most tomograms exhibiting at least partial organized, mesh-like structures (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Vane filaments were observed within the flagellar pocket at the base of the flagellum.
source: We also observed vane filaments within the flagellar pocket at the base of the flagellum (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Previously undescribed barb-like membrane complexes extend ~50 nm from the extracellular surface of the S. rosetta flagellar membrane.
source: In regions of the flagellar membrane adjacent to where the vane filaments protrude, we also observed previously undescribed barb-like membrane complexes, hereafter denoted as 'barbs', that extend ~50 nm from the extracellular surface of the flagellar membrane (Figure 7E-I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7E-I.

claim: Subtomogram averaging of 600 barb particles with fourfold symmetry yielded an average with 2.5 nm resolution.
source: To better resolve the molecular details of these barbs, we performed subtomogram averaging and applied fourfold symmetry resulting in 600 averaged particles that yielded an average with 2.5 nm resolution (0.5 FSC criterion) (Figure 7F–I; Table 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in figures and Table 1.

claim: The barbs consist of a top knob and a central rod with a wider mid-body, from which four arms protrude to connect to the membrane.
source: The barbs consist of a top knob and a central rod with a wider mid-body, from which four arms protrude to connect to the membrane (Figure 7E-I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7E-I.

claim: The number of barbs varied greatly between tomograms, ranging from 0 to 22 barbs.
source: The number of barbs varied greatly between tomograms (which show ~2 µm flagellar length), ranging from 0 to 22 barbs, but their location was consistently near the base of the vane filaments, with a median distance of 50 nm from the barb structures to the vane plane (Figure 7I–K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7I-K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-I.

claim: Barb location was consistently near the base of the vane filaments, with a median distance of 50 nm from the barb structures to the vane plane.
source: The number of barbs varied greatly between tomograms (which show ~2 µm flagellar length), ranging from 0 to 22 barbs, but their location was consistently near the base of the vane filaments, with a median distance of 50 nm from the barb structures to the vane plane (Figure 7I–K, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–I).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7I-K and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-I.

claim: A lumen is visible throughout parts of the central rod of the barbs, but the cavity/channel does not appear to be continuous.
source: Although a lumen is visible throughout parts of the central rod, the cavity/channel does not appear to be continuous, and the base of the rod seems only weakly connected to the membrane, if at all.
evidence: Based on observation of the barb structure.

claim: The base of the barb rod seems only weakly connected to the membrane, if at all.
source: Although a lumen is visible throughout parts of the central rod, the cavity/channel does not appear to be continuous, and the base of the rod seems only weakly connected to the membrane, if at all.
evidence: Based on observation of the barb structure.

claim: Several barb-like structures were observed within the flagellar pocket.
source: We also observed several barb-like structures within the flagellar pocket (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Barb structures were not observed on the surface of 3D reconstructed E. pacifica bacterial cells.
source: The overall shape of the barbs resembles head-less bacteriophages or bacterial secretion needles, but barb structures were not observed on the surface of 3D reconstructed E. pacifica bacterial cells, which were co-cultured with S. rosetta as a food source (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: The structure and organization of the dyneins, radial spokes, and the CPC observed for metazoan flagella are consistent with those of the unicellular choanoflagellate S. rosetta.
source: Here, we find that the structure and organization of the dyneins, radial spokes, and the CPC observed for metazoan flagella are consistent with those of the unicellular choanoflagellate S. rosetta.
evidence: Based on comparison of data from this study with known metazoan structures.

claim: The structural features of dyneins, radial spokes, and CPC were likely present in the urchoanozoan, pre-dating the transition to multicellularity.
source: This suggests that these changes were likely present in the urchoanozoan (the phylogenetic group containing all Choanoflagellates and metazoans), pre-dating the transition to multicellularity.
evidence: Based on inference from the observed similarities between S. rosetta and metazoans.

claim: Most unicellular species contain three outer dynein heads per ODA, whereas flagella from multicellular species typically contain only two.
source: Most unicellular species contain three outer dynein heads (i.e. three dynein heavy chains) per ODA, whereas flagella from multicellular species typically contain only two (Lin et al., 2014; Nicastro et al., 2006; Pigino et al., 2012; Figure 4).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lin et al., 2014; Nicastro et al., 2006; Pigino et al., 2012 and data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The third outer dynein heavy chain was lost in metazoans and most likely independently in excavates.
source: This is consistent with comparative genomic data suggesting that the third outer dynein heavy chain was lost in metazoans and – most likely independently – in excavates (Kollmar, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kollmar, 2016.

claim: Unicellular organisms like Tetrahymena and Chlamydomonas have broad RS head structures and connections between all three radial spoke heads.
source: In addition, unicellular organisms like Tetrahymena and Chlamydomonas have broad RS head structures and connections between all three radial spoke heads, whereas metazoan RS head structures are narrow, RS1 and RS2 are reduced to a pair of thin blades, and RS1 and RS2 are clearly separated from one another (Figure 4; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4 and citations to multiple studies.

claim: Metazoan RS head structures are narrow, RS1 and RS2 are reduced to a pair of thin blades, and RS1 and RS2 are clearly separated from one another.
source: In addition, unicellular organisms like Tetrahymena and Chlamydomonas have broad RS head structures and connections between all three radial spoke heads, whereas metazoan RS head structures are narrow, RS1 and RS2 are reduced to a pair of thin blades, and RS1 and RS2 are clearly separated from one another (Figure 4; Grossman-Haham et al., 2021; Gui et al., 2021; Lin et al., 2014; Zheng et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4 and citations to multiple studies.

claim: The CPC orientation is fixed in metazoans, with stable connections between C1a and C2a and a reduced C1e projection.
source: Furthermore, the CPC orientation is fixed in metazoans, with stable connections between C1a and C2a and a reduced C1e projection (Carbajal-González et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carbajal-González et al., 2013.

claim: Loss of bulkier flagellar structures may have generated space to accommodate additional molecular components in the common ancestor of choanoflagellates and animals.
source: We can speculate that loss of bulkier flagellar structures like the third outer dynein head, broad radial spoke heads, and larger CPC projections may have generated space to accommodate additional molecular components in the common ancestor of choanoflagellates and animals.
evidence: Based on speculation about evolutionary advantages.

claim: Cilia and flagella in animals have adapted many additional signaling functions and molecules compared to free-swimming unicellular eukaryotes like Chlamydomonas.
source: Although free-swimming unicellular eukaryotes like Chlamydomonas also signal through their flagella (sensing light, chemical environmental cues, and mechanosensory stimuli), cilia and flagella in animals have adapted many additional signaling functions and molecules, including T2R, progesterone receptors, estrogen receptor-ß, interleukin-6 receptor, and Hedgehog (HH) pathway components (Bloodgood, 2010; Mitchell, 2007; Sigg et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bloodgood, 2010; Mitchell, 2007; Sigg et al., 2017.

claim: The reduced RS head structures, CPC projections, and dynein motors in S. rosetta could be related to a shift away from predator avoidance toward increased signaling functions in a more stable and protected environment.
source: Could the reduced RS head structures, CPC projections, and dynein motors in S. rosetta be related to a shift away from predator avoidance toward increased signaling functions in a more stable and protected environment?
evidence: Based on speculation about evolutionary pressures.

claim: The additional force provided by three outer dynein arm motors could help counteract the hydrodynamic effects of multiple cilia and flagella in organisms like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena.
source: For example, the additional force provided by three outer dynein arm motors could help counteract the hydrodynamic effects of multiple cilia and flagella in organisms like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena, whereas the evolutionary selection pressure to retain the third outer dynein head may be lost in organisms with only one flagellum.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional advantages.

claim: The evolutionary selection pressure to retain the third outer dynein head may be lost in organisms with only one flagellum.
source: For example, the additional force provided by three outer dynein arm motors could help counteract the hydrodynamic effects of multiple cilia and flagella in organisms like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena, whereas the evolutionary selection pressure to retain the third outer dynein head may be lost in organisms with only one flagellum.
evidence: Based on speculation about evolutionary pressures.

claim: A combination of the rail-MIP and A2-hole may provide the strength and flexibility necessary to compensate for the loss of bulkier flagellar structures in S. rosetta.
source: We report a unique rail-MIP in S. rosetta flagella that runs the length of the A-tubule lumen. MIPs are thought to reinforce structural integrity of doublet microtubules (Owa et al., 2019), therefore a combination of the rail-MIP and A2-hole identified here may provide the strength and flexibility necessary to compensate for the loss of bulkier flagellar structures.
evidence: Based on inference from known MIP function and citation to Owa et al., 2019.

claim: The rail-MIP may provide mechanical support to compensate for external forces such as the extra drag generated by the motion of the flagellar vane.
source: Thus, it is also possible that both the rail-MIP and beak-MIP provide mechanical support to compensate for external forces, such as the extra drag generated by the motion of the flagellar vane (choanoflagellates) or mastigoneme filaments (Chlamydomonas) through the aqueous environment, given both structures' wing-like positioning perpendicular to the beating direction of the flagella.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional roles.

claim: The choanoflagellate flagellar vane has only been observed in a few of the >125 known choanoflagellate species.
source: The choanoflagellate flagellar vane has only been observed in a few of the >125 known choanoflagellate species (Hibberd, 1975; Leadbeater, 2006; Mah et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hibberd, 1975; Leadbeater, 2006; Mah et al., 2014.

claim: Previous reports describe the vane as a bilateral fringe composed of delicate perpendicular fibers of glycocalyx, occasionally with diagonal or longitudinal fibers, which extend approximately two-thirds of the flagellar length.
source: These reports describe the vane as a bilateral fringe composed of delicate perpendicular fibers of glycocalyx, occasionally with diagonal or longitudinal fibers, which extend approximately two-thirds of the flagellar length (Hibberd, 1975; Leadbeater, 2006; Mah et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hibberd, 1975; Leadbeater, 2006; Mah et al., 2014.

claim: The wispy hairs observed in S. rosetta vanes appear similar to the 'partially disintegrated' vanes observed in Monosiga sp.
source: The wispy hairs we observe appear similar to the 'partially disintegrated' vanes observed in Monosiga sp. (Hibberd, 1975), suggesting that they are perhaps not disintegrated but rather a common variation on vane structure.
evidence: Based on comparison with citation to Hibberd, 1975 and inference.

claim: The structure of the choanoflagellate vane differs significantly from other flagellar appendages, including the hair-like mastigonemes from green algae like Chlamydomonas.
source: As has been previously discussed (Hibberd, 1975), the structure of the choanoflagellate vane differs significantly from other flagellar appendages, including the hair-like mastigonemes from green algae like Chlamydomonas (Liu et al., 2020) or the tripartite hairs from golden algae like Ochromonas (Bouck, 1971).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hibberd, 1975; Liu et al., 2020; Bouck, 1971.

claim: Algal mastigonemes are comprised of two intertwined filaments with an overall diameter of ~10 nm and organized as single or tripartite hairs.
source: Both the size and arrangement of filaments is distinct, with algal mastigonemes comprised of two intertwined filaments with an overall diameter of ~10 nm and organized as single or tripartite hairs (Liu et al., 2020), vs choanoflagellate filament diameters of ~3.5 nm arranged as wispy hairs or meshed networks.
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Choanoflagellate vane filament diameters are ~3.5 nm arranged as wispy hairs or meshed networks.
source: Both the size and arrangement of filaments is distinct, with algal mastigonemes comprised of two intertwined filaments with an overall diameter of ~10 nm and organized as single or tripartite hairs (Liu et al., 2020), vs choanoflagellate filament diameters of ~3.5 nm arranged as wispy hairs or meshed networks.
evidence: Based on data from this study.

claim: No connections were detected between the membrane anchor of the choanoflagellate vane filaments and the axonemal microtubules.
source: In addition, we do not detect connections between the membrane anchor of the choanoflagellate vane filaments and the axonemal microtubules, in contrast to observations for Chlamydomonas and Euglena (Liu et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on data from this study and citation to Liu et al., 2020.

claim: Homologues of the mastigoneme protein MST1 and membrane anchor PKD2 were not detected in the S. rosetta genome via BLAST search.
source: Consistent with these morphological differences, we also did not detect homologues of the mastigoneme protein MST1 and membrane anchor PKD2 in the S. rosetta genome via BLAST search, suggesting that the vane differs from these flagellar appendages.
evidence: Based on data from BLAST search analysis.

claim: The morphology of the choanoflagellate vane is similar to the bilateral, wing-like vane of sponge choanocyte flagella.
source: Instead, it was proposed that the morphology of the choanoflagellate vane is similar to the bilateral, wing-like vane of sponge choanocyte flagella, which is anchored in the flagellar membrane without connections to the axonemal microtubules (Mehl and Reiswig, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mehl and Reiswig, 1991.

claim: Sponge choanocyte vanes appear to be narrower, denser, and more massive than choanoflagellate vanes.
source: However, sponge choanocyte vanes appear to be narrower, denser, and more massive than choanoflagellate vanes, and they often connect laterally to the collar microvilli (Brunet and King, 2017; Hibberd, 1975; Leadbeater, 2006; Mah et al., 2014; Mehl and Reiswig, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: The choanoflagellate vane has previously been reported to span the width of the collar in Monosiga brevicolis.
source: The choanoflagellate vane has previously been reported to span the width of the collar in Monosiga brevicolis (Mah et al., 2014), however, the field of view in our tomograms does note capture the ends of the vane to assess any potential connections to the microvilli.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mah et al., 2014.

claim: Fibers originate within the flagellar pocket, suggesting the possibility that the vane could be secreted from the cell membrane before being transported into the flagellar compartment.
source: Though our data do not directly address these questions, we do observe fibers that originate within the flagellar pocket, suggesting the possibility that the vane could be secreted from the cell membrane before being transported into the flagellar compartment (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on inference from data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Large, fiber-filled vesicles have been observed near the apical part of choanoflagellate cells following division, presumably when the flagellum and vane would be regenerating.
source: Though not present in our cryo-ET data of fast and slow swimmers, large, fiber-filled vesicles have been observed near the apical part of choanoflagellate cells following division, presumably when the flagellum and vane would be regenerating (Leadbeater, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Leadbeater, 2014.

claim: Glycosyltransferases such as those encoded by jumble and couscous localize to both the basal pole and the flagellar/collar base.
source: Intriguingly, glycosyltransferases such as those encoded by jumble and couscous localize to both the basal pole and the flagellar/collar base, and the collar base also stains positively for jacalin, Lycopersicon esculentum (tomato) lectin (LEL), and Solanum tuberosum (potato) lectin (STL), indicating the presence of carbohydrate chains made of Galß3GalNAc and GlcNAc2-4 near the choanoflagellate flagellum (Wetzel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wetzel et al., 2018.

claim: The collar base stains positively for jacalin, LEL, and STL, indicating the presence of carbohydrate chains made of Galß3GalNAc and GlcNAc2-4 near the choanoflagellate flagellum.
source: Intriguingly, glycosyltransferases such as those encoded by jumble and couscous localize to both the basal pole and the flagellar/collar base, and the collar base also stains positively for jacalin, Lycopersicon esculentum (tomato) lectin (LEL), and Solanum tuberosum (potato) lectin (STL), indicating the presence of carbohydrate chains made of Galß3GalNAc and GlcNAc2-4 near the choanoflagellate flagellum (Wetzel et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wetzel et al., 2018.

claim: External digest with proteinase K failed to remove the flagellar vane, supporting the hypothesis that the S. rosetta flagellar vane is carbohydrate or glycoprotein-based rather than proteinaceous.
source: We performed an external digest with proteinase K, which failed to remove the flagellar vane (data not shown), supporting the hypothesis that the S. rosetta flagellar vane is carbohydrate or glycoprotein-based rather than proteinaceous, though additional study is necessary to further characterize the specific vane component(s).
evidence: Based on experimental data (proteinase K digest) and inference.

claim: The barbs' location alongside the flagellar vane suggests that they could play a role in vane generation or maintenance.
source: The barbs' location alongside the flagellar vane suggests that they could play a role in vane generation or maintenance.
evidence: Based on speculation about functional roles.

claim: The top knobs at the barbs' distal ends resemble the size and shape of the nodes within the proximal vane.
source: Indeed, the top knobs at the barbs' distal ends resemble the size and shape of the nodes within the proximal vane, though the distance to the flagellar membrane in the vane base is roughly twice that of the barb height.
evidence: Based on comparison of structural features.

claim: The S. rosetta genome has undergone extensive horizontal gene transfer from bacteria and other organisms.
source: However, the S. rosetta genome has undergone extensive horizontal gene transfer from bacteria and other organisms (Matriano et al., 2021), so it is possible that the barbs could have an ancient bacterial origin.
evidence: Supported by citation to Matriano et al., 2021.

claim: The barb structures most closely resemble the size, shape, and general distribution of an uncharacterized bacterial complex in Prosthecobacter debontii.
source: Indeed, the barb structures most closely resemble the size, shape, and general distribution of an uncharacterized bacterial complex in Prosthecobacter debontii, although the bacterial structures exhibit a fivefold rather than fourfold symmetry (Dobro et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Dobro et al., 2017.

claim: Choanoflagellate flagella more closely resemble human flagella than other protist model systems like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena.
source: Furthermore, because choanoflagellate flagella more closely resemble human flagella, they may represent an attractive alternative to other protist model systems like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena for the study of human ciliopathies.
evidence: Based on inference from structural similarities observed in this study.

claim: Choanoflagellates may represent an attractive alternative to other protist model systems for the study of human ciliopathies.
source: Furthermore, because choanoflagellate flagella more closely resemble human flagella, they may represent an attractive alternative to other protist model systems like Chlamydomonas and Tetrahymena for the study of human ciliopathies.
evidence: Based on speculation about potential research applications.

claim: S. rosetta was co-cultured with E. pacifica as a food source.
source: S. rosetta co-cultured with E. pacifica was obtained from ATCC (PRA-390) and was cultured as previously described (King lab choanoflagellate handbook: https://kinglab.berkeley.edu/resources/, Levin and King, 2013).
evidence: Supported by methods description and citation to Levin and King, 2013.

claim: Cryo-FIB milling was performed using a 30 keV gallium ion beam with currents of 30 pA for initial bulk milling and thinning, and 10 pA for final polishing.
source: For milling, the cryo-stage was tilted to a shallow angle of 11–18 degrees between the EM grid and the gallium ion beam. Cryo-FIB milling was performed using a 30 keV gallium ion beam with currents of 30 pA for initial bulk milling and thinning, and 10 pA for final polishing, resulting in ~150-nm-thick, self-supporting lamella.
evidence: Supported by methods description.

claim: Tilt series images were collected using a K3 Summit direct electron detector at ×26,000 magnification under low-dose conditions in counting mode.
source: Tilt series images were collected using a K3 Summit direct electron detector (Gatan) at ×26,000 magnification and under low-dose conditions and in counting mode (for each tilt series image: 10 frames, 0.05 s per frame, dose rate of ~28 e/pixel/s, frames were recorded in super-res mode and then binned by 2, resulting in a pixel size of 3.15 Å).
evidence: Supported by methods description.

claim: The cumulative electron dose per tilt series was limited to 100 e-/Å2.
source: The cumulative electron dose per tilt series was limited to 100 e-/Å2.
evidence: Supported by methods description.
